title: MX and NS Records: The Mail Room and the Management Office
content:
Let's be clear about something before we go further.

When you send an email to someone@meridian-financial.com, your email client does not know the IP address of Meridian Financial's mail server. All it knows is the domain: meridian-financial.com. So how does your email actually get delivered?

It asks DNS. And DNS answers with the MX record.

**The MX Record: The Mail Room Address**

The MX record (Mail Exchange record) specifies which server is responsible for receiving email for a domain.

**What it is**: An MX record contains two pieces of information — a priority value (a number) and a mail server hostname. Example: '10 aspmx.l.google.com.' Priority 10. Mail server: aspmx.l.google.com.

**Why it exists**: Email uses SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), and SMTP servers need to know where to deliver mail. Before MX records existed, the only option was to try the A record of the domain — which was far too limiting. MX records were created specifically to separate 'which server handles this domain's web traffic' from 'which server handles this domain's email.' They are different servers. They need different answers.

**The priority value**: MX records have a priority number. Lower numbers mean higher priority. An organisation can list multiple MX records with different priorities — the sending server tries the lowest number first, and falls back to higher-numbered servers if the primary is unavailable.

Example:
10 aspmx.l.google.com (primary mail server)
20 alt1.aspmx.l.google.com (backup)
30 alt2.aspmx.l.google.com (backup)

**What it reveals professionally**:

— 'aspmx.l.google.com' → Google Workspace (Gmail for Business). The organisation uses Google for email. Phishing simulations should target Google login pages. Credential harvesting attacks should be designed for Google accounts.

— 'mail.protection.outlook.com' → Microsoft 365 / Exchange Online. Phishing templates should mimic Microsoft login flows.

— 'mx.zoho.com' → Zoho Mail. Less common, worth noting.

— 'mail.meridian-financial.com' → Self-hosted mail server. The organisation runs its own email server, and that server has an IP address you can look up. Mail servers using SMTP communicate directly with each other — there is no CDN equivalent for email delivery. The IP address of a self-hosted mail server is almost always a real server IP, directly reachable from the internet.

**The analogy**: If domain.com is a company building, the MX record is the address of their mail room — not a PO box, but the actual room where physical post arrives. When you know where the mail room is, you know something real about the company's internal infrastructure.

---

**The NS Record: The Management Office**

The NS record (Nameserver record) specifies which nameservers are authoritative for the domain — which servers hold the official, definitive copy of all DNS records for this domain.

**What it is**: NS records list the hostnames of the servers that answer DNS queries about this domain. When a resolver asks 'what is the IP address of meridian-financial.com?', it is ultimately asking one of the nameservers listed in the NS records.

**Why it exists**: The DNS hierarchy requires each domain to declare which servers are authoritative for it. Without NS records, the TLD nameserver would have no way to refer resolver queries to the right place. NS records are the 'please direct all further questions to this office' sign in the DNS system.

**What it reveals professionally**:

— 'ns1.cloudflare.com' → DNS managed through Cloudflare. Strong signal that Cloudflare is also proxying their web traffic. Any changes to DNS go through Cloudflare's interface — their account security directly affects their entire DNS zone.

— 'ns-xxx.awsdns-xx.com' → DNS managed through AWS Route 53. The infrastructure is likely on AWS.

— 'ns1.digitalocean.com' → DNS through DigitalOcean.

— 'ns1.meridian-financial.com' → The organisation manages its own nameservers. Custom nameservers mean the organisation runs DNS infrastructure itself — likely on-premises or on a dedicated server they control. This is also the server you attempt zone transfer requests against in a professional engagement — and self-managed nameservers have historically been more likely to be misconfigured.

**The analogy**: NS records are the management office reception. If you want any official information about this building — who lives here, what their address is, what services they run — the reception desk tells you which office keeps the records. The NS record does the same for DNS: it tells you which servers are authorised to answer questions about this domain.

callouts.title: MX Record Intelligence in Practice
callouts.text:
The MX record is one of the most consistently useful DNS records in a professional engagement.

For a penetration tester: it determines which email platform phishing simulations should be designed for.

For a red teamer: a self-hosted mail server IP is often a real, directly accessible server that bypasses CDN protection — a direct path to origin infrastructure.

For a bug bounty hunter: the mail server hostname frequently contains the server version or product name, which can lead to CVE research.

For a defender: regularly auditing your own MX records to confirm they point to intended destinations — and have appropriate backup MX records configured — is a basic email security hygiene task.

callouts.title: NS Records and Account Compromise
callouts.text:
If an attacker gains access to the account where a domain's NS records are managed — the Cloudflare account, the AWS Route 53 account, the domain registrar account — they can change every DNS record for the domain. They can redirect the website to their own server. They can change the MX record to intercept all email. They can add TXT records to verify domain ownership with new cloud services.

This is called DNS hijacking. It is one of the most devastating attacks on an organisation's internet presence — and it starts by compromising the account that manages the NS records. Knowing which provider manages a target's DNS (from the NS records) tells you where their critical account security lives.

keyTerms.definition: Mail Exchange record. Specifies which servers handle incoming email for the domain, with priority values determining the order of preference. Reveals email provider (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, self-hosted). Self-hosted MX records frequently point to real server IPs not protected by CDN.

Nameserver record. Specifies which servers are authoritative for the domain's DNS zone — the official source of all DNS records. Reveals DNS hosting provider (Cloudflare, AWS Route 53, self-managed). The nameservers listed here are the targets of zone transfer requests.

A numeric value on each MX record that determines delivery order. Lower numbers have higher priority. A domain with multiple MX records at different priority values has email failover configured — the sending server tries the lowest priority number first, then falls back to higher numbers.
